summary: As Jesus dies, the temple veil tears from top to bottom and a Roman centurion confesses Him; soldiers find Him already dead and pierce His side.
key_insight: Mark mentions no earthquake. His centurion spoke when he “saw that He cried out like this and breathed His last.” The way Jesus died was enough to convince the officer in charge of killing Him.
story: Then the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. The earth quaked and the rocks were split. The graves were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised; after Jesus’ resurrection they came out of the graves, went into the holy city and appeared to many. {Mt}

The centurion who stood opposite Jesus saw how He cried out and breathed His last. {Mk} He and the soldiers with him saw the earthquake and all that had happened, and they feared greatly. {Mt} The centurion said, “Truly this Man was the Son of God!” {Mk} Luke records that he glorified God, saying, “Certainly this was a righteous Man!” {Lk}

The whole crowd that had come together to see it beat their breasts and went home. {Lk} All Jesus’ acquaintances stood at a distance, {Lk} with the women who had followed Him from Galilee and served Him, and many other women who had come up with Him to Jerusalem. Among them were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses. {Mk} Mark also names Salome, {Mk} and Matthew the mother of Zebedee’s sons. {Mt}

It was the Preparation Day, and the coming Sabbath was a high day. So that the bodies would not remain on the crosses on the Sabbath, the Jewish leaders asked Pilate to have the men’s legs broken and the bodies taken away. {Jn}

The soldiers broke the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. But when they came to Jesus and saw that He was already dead, they did not break His legs. Instead one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. {Jn}

The one who saw it has testified, and his testimony is true, “so that you may believe.” These things fulfilled the Scriptures: “Not one of His bones shall be broken,” and, “They shall look on Him whom they pierced.” {Jn}
differences: Only Matthew tells of the earthquake, the split rocks, the opened graves and the saints raised.
Matthew and Mark record the centurion saying Jesus was the Son of God; Luke records, “Certainly this was a righteous Man!” Matthew includes the soldiers with him and says they feared greatly.
Mark names Salome among the women; Matthew names the mother of Zebedee’s sons; Luke adds Jesus’ acquaintances and the crowd beating their breasts.
Only John tells of the broken legs, the spear, the blood and water, and his own eyewitness testimony.
Here the women watch “from afar”; earlier John placed Jesus’ mother and other women “by the cross” (John 19:25).

fit.question: Matthew and Mark record the centurion saying, “Truly this was the Son of God!” Luke has, “Certainly this was a righteous Man!” What did he say?

points.label: More than one sentence
points.text: Luke says the centurion “glorified God.” A frightened man praising God after such a death may well have said more than one thing, and the writers chose the words that served their accounts.

points.label: Luke’s line of witnesses
points.text: All through the trial Luke stresses that Jesus was innocent. Pilate said so three times (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), Herod found nothing deserving death (23:15), and the dying criminal said, “this Man has done nothing wrong” (23:41). The centurion’s “righteous” completes that line.

points.label: What a soldier meant
points.text: A Roman officer may not have grasped all that Christians mean by “Son of God.” But he had heard the mockers repeat that Jesus claimed to be the Son of God (Matthew 27:40, 43), and the Gospels record his words because they were true beyond what he knew.

fit.note: Two witnesses report different words from the same man. Each fits, and together they show what the cross made plain even to a pagan officer.
fit.short: The centurion likely said more than one thing; Luke highlights “righteous,” the last of many witnesses to Jesus’ innocence.

fit.question: John says Jesus’ mother and other women stood “by the cross” (John 19:25). Matthew, Mark and Luke say the women watched from a distance. Which is right?

points.label: Two moments
points.text: John probably describes a time before the darkness, when Jesus spoke to His mother and the beloved disciple. The other Gospels describe the end, after Jesus died. The women may have come near for a time and later stood farther off.

points.label: Mary taken home
points.text: John says that “from that hour” the disciple took Jesus’ mother to his own home (19:27). The later lists of women do not name her, which fits her having left before the end.

fit.note: The accounts describe different points in the long hours on the cross; there is no conflict between them.
fit.short: John describes the women near the cross earlier; the others describe them at a distance at the end, probably after Jesus’ mother had left.

scene.label: The veil
scene.text: A great curtain hung before the Most Holy Place, the inner room of the temple. Only the high priest went behind it, once a year on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). Most take this to be the curtain that was torn, and both Matthew and Mark say it tore “from top to bottom.”

scene.label: The ninth hour
scene.text: Jesus died about three in the afternoon, the hour of prayer when the afternoon sacrifice was offered (Acts 3:1). Priests would have been at work in the temple when the curtain tore.

scene.label: Breaking the legs
scene.text: A crucified man could live for a long time. Breaking his legs took away the support of his body and brought death quickly. The leaders asked for it because the Sabbath was near, and this Sabbath was a “high day,” falling in Passover week.

scene.label: Blood and water
scene.text: John insists he saw it himself. A spear thrust that brought out blood and water left no doubt that Jesus was dead. Medical explanations differ; John’s point is that the death was real and that he was a witness.

scene.label: No bone broken
scene.text: The Passover lamb was to be eaten without breaking any of its bones (Exodus 12:46), and Psalm 34:20 says of the righteous man, “Not one of them is broken.” Zechariah 12:10 foretold that Israel would one day “look on Me whom they pierced.”

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew tells of the earthquake, the split rocks and the saints raised, signs that the King’s death shook creation and broke the hold of the grave. He notes that the saints came out “after His resurrection,” so that their appearing in the city followed His rising.
witnesses.mark: In Mark the centurion is the first human being to call Jesus the Son of God; until now only the Father and the unclean spirits have said it (1:11; 3:11). Mark began his book with “Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1), and a Gentile soldier says it at the cross.
witnesses.luke: Luke’s centurion glorifies God and calls Jesus righteous, and the crowds go home beating their breasts. Luke alone mentions Jesus’ “acquaintances” standing with the women, witnesses who would soon see Him alive.
witnesses.john: John alone tells of the broken legs and the spear, and he steps forward as an eyewitness: “his testimony is true.” He writes “so that you may believe,” and links the unbroken bones to the Passover lamb, fitting his picture of Jesus as “The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world” (1:29).

seeing.reveals: Jesus’ death opened the way to God. The curtain that kept all but the high priest out of God’s presence was torn when He died, and the first to confess Him afterward was a Gentile soldier.
seeing.living: Believers now have “boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). Do not stand at a distance from God as though the curtain were still hanging. Come near through Christ in prayer and confession, with confidence.
seeing.ponder: Do you still pray as if the veil were hanging between you and God?

preaching.big_idea: When Jesus died, the way to God tore open, and even His executioners confessed Him.
outline: The veil torn from top to bottom (51a)
The earth shaken and the graves opened (51b–53)
preaching.watch_for: The mockers had said, “If You are the Son of God,” and sneered that He had claimed it (27:40, 43). Matthew lets Roman soldiers answer the taunt: “Truly this was the Son of God!” (27:54).
